items.text: Funding for the Smithsonian Jazz Oral History Program NEA Jazz Master interview was provided by the National Endowment for the Arts.
MELBA LISTON
NEA Jazz Master (1987)
Interviewee: Melba Liston (January 13, 1926 – April 23, 1999)
Interviewer: Clora Bryant
Description: Transcript, 68 pp.
Transcriber’s note: This interview of Melba Liston dates from 1996. Liston had suffered a stroke in 1985. Thereafter she had some loss of memory and some difficulty speaking.

Quotations appear below in the normal manner found throughout transcripts from the Smithsonian’s series of jazz oral histories, but exceptionally, for those passages in which Liston has difficulty responding, square brackets identify a summary of contents standing in place of a full quotation.
[The recording commences in mid-sentence:]

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: . . . Jazz Oral History Program, and today’s date is December 4th, 1996. We’re here at the home of Miss Melba Liston – here in Los Angeles, that is – and we’re going to do an interview about her life. My name is Clora Bryant. I will be doing the interview with Melba, and we have Matt [Watson as recording engineer]. First we want to start out by asking Melba where she’s from originally.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I was born in Kansas City, Missouri, and my grandparents lived in Kansas City, Kansas, so I was between both of them.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: You stayed – during the week you’d stay with your grandparents and then on the weekends you’d stay with your mom. [Liston went to school in Kansas City, Kansas, while living with her grandfather.]

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: [Her mother’s name was Lucille Liston. Her grandparents were Virginia and John Clark. Liston could not remember what her mother and grandparents did, but recalled that her mother went to college]. I think maybe that’s why we moved out here, because she wasn’t getting no business in Kansas.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: She was overqualified for the work that she was getting.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: But you have no sisters or brothers.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: No.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: At your home, I know you said you had a piano – a piano-roll piano. So you were exposed to that. And you had a radio, and you were exposed to the music that you heard that was being played around Kansas City. And also, your grandfather listened to – did he have records or something?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: No. We didn’t have records at that time. We had the player. This is my – this is the same piano.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: That’s the same piano. Wow!

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: But it had legs on it. It had really big feet – lovely feet on it. All that stuff.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Did you sit there and pedal it.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah, and my aunties would dance.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Thelma too?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: But your mother? Did she dance too?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Nah. I don’t think so. I don’t remember her dancing.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: [asks about the family’s economic situation in Kansas City during the Depression.]

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: [cannot remember]. But we didn’t have no problems.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: All of you attended church.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Did you sing in church? Is that where you started singing? Because you do sing.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Once in a while.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Okay. But when you were little, did you sing in the children’s choir or something?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: No. Not in no choir.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: No. Just sing in church. Okay. With the congregation.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah. And when I’m home, the radio.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: You sing with the radio?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Um-hmm.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Most jazz musicians started in church. That’s why I’m trying to get to that. Watson: What church were you in?

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: [names various denominations.]

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Unity.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: [asks about music Liston heard, including Count Basie and Cab Calloway.]

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: My pop’s favorite was Cab Calloway. My auntie’s loved [Jimmie] Lunceford and Basie.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: [asks about Liston starting music at the age of 3 or 4.]

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: [cannot recall.]

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: [At the age of 7 Liston saw a trombone and asked her mother to get it that same day. Bryant had the same reaction to the trumpet. Did her mother spoil her?]

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: No. I’ve got a record – I mean a tape with my mother’s voice on there, and she’s talking about when I first got my horn.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Really? You should have let me hear that. [Bryant states her intention to hear this tape before the interview resumes the next day.] The other day I mentioned about the system that you had, that you – where you could pick out the melody of songs by the number of the note or the scale, and that your teachers thought you were a genius, and the church members too thought you were a genius, because you could do that. But it’s something that your little mind told you – which was great. But you say that you like to puzzle things, because you like math.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I like mathematics, but I used to like to hear things, and I would say “2 - 4 – 6” or something.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: [inquires into this method, but without much response from Liston. Bryant inquires about Liston’s friends.]

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I got a whole lot of friends, I guess, but I didn’t go around with anything. I was with my grandpa on the back porch, playing the trombone.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: [Liston said she was playing Deep River and Rocking the Cradle of the Deep. Were these her choice or her grandfather’s?]

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I heard them on the radio.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: [Liston said the day before that she was playing these melodies five months after she got her trombone.] You found that you couldn’t reach the sixth and the seventh position on it, but you overcame that by . . .

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: . . . turning my head sideways. I had to do that until I come out here to California.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: And then your arms became long enough, or what?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I was growing. I guess I grew out of that before I went with Mrs. Hightower.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: [Liston had a teacher in Kansas City that she didn’t like.]

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I told my mother to cancel him. So we didn’t stay – two or three lessons, that was all. [She cannot recall the reasons why.]

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: In 1937 all of a sudden the family moved to California. You and your mom?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: No. My mom and me stayed over, and my grandma and my aunties moved out here. Maybe four or five months later, we came out. I don’t really know the exact times.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: [asks about the trip to California.]

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: [remembers only that it was a train ride.]

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: When you got here, then you enrolled in McKinley Junior High School.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: But yesterday you were saying that the teacher’s were – you passed a test to be in the ninth grade?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah. They couldn’t put me in the ninth grade. They put me in the eighth grade anyway, but I was only 10 or something, so they couldn’t put me. I could have passed a test for [ . . . ] going on high school.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: You’re kidding!

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: But I couldn’t go there, because I was too young. But there’s a lot of things that I didn’t know, anyway. Growing up, you don’t know about a lot of things, and I had to learn about self things and all of those things before I got to high school.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: But in music – they had music there, and you had a teacher?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Oh yeah.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: He was good?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Mr. [(name inaudible) ?Doddard Deal].

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: First time I heard the name.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I looked it up. He was good. He didn’t mess with me. He just was a good teacher for all around. [Liston has difficulty describing his musical specialization.]

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: But he wanted to adopt you?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: He wanted to send me to some places, and I didn’t want to go, but he wanted me – he would have to adopt me to send me to all of these places. I can’t remember now. Anyway, I told him, “No. I want to stay with my mom.”

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: When you guys got out here, you did continue your church affiliation, right?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yes.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: You started playing your horn in church?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: No.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Not right away?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I didn’t play my horn in church, unless they were getting some Christmas and New Year’s and all of that stuff. I didn’t play every Sunday.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: We forgot about your radio show in Kansas.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: [cannot recall details.] I was a little star.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: But it was just you and the piano then?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Back to L.A. At school you met Minnie Hightower?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: And she was the one that told you about Mrs. Hightower.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: [cannot recall.] I met her, and she was thrilled with my playing the trombone and all that. We had a good thing going for many years. We played everywhere. We practiced at the Ross Snyder playground. [At night in the summertime they played in the parks.]

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Do you remember some of the people besides Minnie and Vi Redd?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Alice Young. Those three, we were close. I don’t think no other girls were in there at the time. And boys . . .

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Were you the only trombone player?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: [cannot recall.]

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: I know in the pictures you’re the only one. You have the pictures. [Bryant refers to describes a photograph in which Liston and Vi Redd are wearing socks.] But when you went to the fair – I wanted to ask you about that.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: We rode up and back in a truck in the back seat – I mean the back of a truck. Miss Hightower and the truck driver was up in the front. We made it. I guess that was my first time on the road. We played – I don’t know what year that was.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: You remember the name of the group, though.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Melodic Dots. Miss Hightower and the Melodic Dots. Oh dear.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Was 1938 something like the year?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Uh-huh.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: What-all did Miss Hightower teach you guys?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Everything. Everything dancers do. Everything horns do. Everything everybody did. We did dancing and – tap dancing and hula dancing. Did everything. Everything that was on the stage, she taught us

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: You did skits?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah. I can’t remember who. Paul Robeson or somebody. She would take us through things like he did, or somebody like that. [Liston cannot remember details.]

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: But she taught you theory, harmony?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Not harmony. Theory, yes. A little bit of it, anyway.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: But she taught you to read?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I was reading already.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: But I mean the kids in the band?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: [cannot recall.] I remember she would let me go out and play or something while she would do some other things with the kids. [Again, Liston does not recall the details.] But she didn’t teach, because I was reading all the time.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Miss Hightower seemed to have had quite an attachment. She thought you were just the greatest.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I don’t know about that.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: It’s been said.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: She was nice to me. I stayed with her until 16 and I joined the union and started to work at the Lincoln Theater. I think she was kind of pissed off with me then. But anyway, that started me on the road to where I am now.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: But at the Lincoln, some of the other kids went there with you, from the Melodic Dots?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Alice Young. Her name’s Mrs. H[?(inaudible)] or something now. But she – nobody else.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: But there were – you said that when Bardu [Ali] thought you . . .

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I guess he thought I was from college or something, because the acts that would come in that didn’t have any music, he would say, “Girl, write the music for it,” and I would write it. So I started writing.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: You started that in high school.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I think I did some writing in high school, but not for a band like that. I was writing for bands – 12, 13, 14, 15 pieces, something like that. That was the start of my writing career.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: That was the beginning of that. Bardu had been with Chick Webb?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah, he did.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: So did you guys play any of Chick Webb’s music in the band?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: [cannot recall.]

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: [read that somewhere.] But you had mentioned yesterday that you would do some skits sometimes with Pigmeat Markum?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah. Pigmeat Markum was always there. He had the run of the show. When he had some skit to do that wasn’t around the action on the stage, I would go on and do them. But Miss Hightower taught us how to do that anyway, so it wasn’t no big thing. I wasn’t thrilled about nothing. I just did everything that you could do when you’re on the stage or in the pit band.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: You had said that sometimes there was an actor who would come on and do a serious type of skit and then Pigmeat would come along and . . .

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: [Laughs]. Oh yeah. He would come on and do it afterwards. Oh dear. That was something else.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Like slapstick or something?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah, something like that. I don’t know how you could call it, but he would come on and really just do it up.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: He destroyed the legitimate thing.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: That must have been an education, working with him.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah, it was. And Dusty Fletcher. He and Dusty Fletcher had a run all the time. Singers – I can’t remember all the singers.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: What’s the girl who was with Lucky Millinder, married Marl Young? Didn’t she sing – I saw her there. Not Joya Sherill.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: [knows Marl, but cannot recall the singer’s name.]

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: [asks about Valaida Snow.]

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: [cannot recall details.] I had a year or a year and a half there, so everybody came through there.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Herb Jeffries?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah. That was it in 19 – whatever it is – 40. We had our thing, and then whitey had his thing.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: You mean downtown at the Million Dollar and all that.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Um-hmm. Sometimes they would work downtown and then come to the Lincoln and do it. It was nice.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Then when Gerald Wilson . . .

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: He says he stole me out of the band.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: That’s what he said.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: So I guess he did. I worked with him. I was saying 5 or 6, but he said 8 years. That’s a long time. We worked everywhere. We worked Chicago, New York, and everything. I was the copyist and sometime I would do the arrangements.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: You learned a lot from him?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah, yeah. He said he learned a lot. We just had a good thing going.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Back and forth? But your first job, you said, with him was at Shepp’s Playhouse.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Remember how that came about?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: [cannot recall.]

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: [gives Liston prompts naming bandmembers who came with Liston from Bardu Ali to Gerald Wilson: Vernon Slater, Jimmy Bunn, Floyd Turner. She asks if they left Shepp’s and went on the road. ]

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: [They went to New York.]

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: [They played in the same show with Jimmie Lunceford.]

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: [But they were never as prominent in California.] I don’t think it’s jazz orientation. I’m going back to New York. [laughter]

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: To get that feeling again.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yes, indeed.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Do you think by following Jimmie Lunceford, that’s why you guys played so good back there too?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: No, we just had a good band.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Competition, I mean. Do you think competition . . .

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: No. We just had a good band. We didn’t have no competition with nobody. We just had a good band, and we knew it. We knew we had a good band. Maybe we got a little over-pretentious or something.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Egotistical.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: No. We just had a good band, and we knew it. That’s all. I would go out and sing and blow my horn.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: On the show at the Apollo?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah. Everywhere we went, because they would say, “Let the girl do something.” Gerald said, “Melba, write something up and do it.” So I did what he said.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: When you left New York, was that the time that Dizzy [Gillespie] asked you to come up and play? The first time? That wasn’t the time?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: No. That was a year – years. We had worked together for a long time before Dizzy. Gerald knew him, but I don’t think we knew him at all up until almost the bebop era.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: So then you left the Apollo and came back to L.A. then.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Oh yeah. Stopped here and there. Maybe Chicago and Kansas and everywhere. We went to – I had a band that went to – Lady Day. We were . . .

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Billie Holiday.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: . . . Yeah, behind Lady Day. It was in the South somewhere.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: South Carolina? Greens . . . Oh that’s where – you got stranded there.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: There wasn’t nothing happening.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: They didn’t like Billie?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I don’t know. But she left and we were stranded on the bus, and Gerald took all the money that we had and gave it to the fellows to get back home, and we just had enought to get us to Kansas City. [Liston cannot recall what happened next.]

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Did you become disillusioned?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Not at that time. I had maybe 6 or 7 or 8 years before I was [disillusioned].

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: But when you came back, is that when you had work with smaller groups and had to stand up and jam all night or something?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Oh yeah. That was a mess. Mainly, though, I would just stay in the background and play the parts, and saxophone and trumpet played the solos, but, like I said, the girl has to do something, so I had to do something once in a while.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Was that after you and Gerald had been with Basie? When you came back from New York?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: [cannot recall the chronology.]

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Gerald said that you recorded with Basie and that the record is out now, on CD.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: [does not know about it or remember recording with Basie.]

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: He also was saying that in – was it in his band, who he hired? No. After Basie, you guys went with Dizzy the first time? He went and you went together? That’s when they had John Coltrane?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I went, and Dizzy found a spot for him to go, but that was in the wintertime. [She cannot remember the name of the club.] I didn’t know how to get there. Gerald was out of town. I had finished my work. I said, damn, I got to get to see Dizzy. I don’t want to have to sit down here and do nothing. So I asked somebody how to get downtown. I was living uptown. He said, “You go down in the subway, and when you get to 49th Street, you come up, and you’ll be there.” That sure was there. Right on the corner. Billy Eckstine was out front. He said, “…, where you been? We’ve been looking for you. Dizzy’s had the chair empty for a whole week.” I said, “Oh, man.” And I didn’t have my trombone. It was a thing. I had to – Dizzy had to rent a trombone or something, and I had to get the guys’ uniform. I had to put that on, and it was leaning all – it was terrible. My mom sent my horn, and it worked out all right.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Was that scary or exciting? Was it exciting?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Nothing was scary, or nothing like that. It was just a drag. He was looking for me, and I didn’t know about it, and then had to go and get this horn that I didn’t . . .

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Mouthpiece?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I don’t know if a mouthpiece made any difference. And the uniform and everything like that.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Is that the band with John Coltrane in it?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Um-hmm.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: [asks if there were any resentments or jealously in the band.]

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: [does not think so.]

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: [names other bandmembers: John Collins, Jimmie Heath, Specs Wright, Al McKibbon, Willie Cook, John Lewis. She asks about the bop style and about the other trombone players in the band.]

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: [recalls that one of the bandmembers told her some things about the bop style, but she cannot recall details. She does not remember the other trombonists.]

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: I was just wondering, what chair did you take?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: There were three ’bones. I guess we mixed it all up. [The bass trombonist played that part all the time; the other two switched parts.]

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: [Liston said the previous day that the band stayed together for five months and then broke up.]

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Oh yeah, because there wasn’t no jobs for us. Nothing for us to do but come on home.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Came back to L.A. Then?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Back to Gerald and all that stuff.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: He had come back already?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Uh-huh.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Was that when you went into the Board of Education?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: [cannot recall.]

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Because you got tired of the road.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Not so much tired of it.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: The conditions, I mean.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah, the conditions.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Who encouraged you to take the exam.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Nobody. I was good at math and all that, so I said, I’m through with this road business. I’m going to take – I think I took it on my own. I knew I was going to pass. There’s nothing new to me.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: [asks how Liston’s mother felt about it.]

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: [Everything was all right.]

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: [asks what Liston did there. Clerical?]

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: [Yes. It was night school.] I did take some gigs. I was gigging after a while, because the thing was envy, I guess. [The conversation takes a confusing turn from Liston’s Board of Education job, which may have been at Jefferson High School, to her high school years, briefly at Jefferson but mainly at Polytechnic High School, with Minnie Hightower.]

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: [Liston worked at the Board of Education for three years.]

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Maybe two, three years. But I would take off now and then for . . .

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: For gigs, you mean.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Not no steady. Once in a while. Just a night or two. Then I quit that, and I went to playing again, and that didn’t – no, it’s not working. And so I went to work at the insurance company, Adams . . .

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Adams and Western? Golden State.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah. I went there.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: I didn’t know that.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: And I would go – on my lunch thing, I would go in my car and listen to some . . .

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Feel the music.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: [does not recall how long she worked there.]

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: But before that we also forgot Dexter Gordon.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: He and I were in school together. He was a bad, bad tenor player, all the time. He was breaking this record. I said, “I’m not – no, no.” He said, “Come on.”

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: What’d he call you?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: You know.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: His favorite word?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yes sir. That was the first time I had played without any music. Oh, Lordy. That was terrible.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: You sounded good. [Does Liston remember any of the other guys on that session in 1947?]

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: [does not recall.]

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: [Liston had not recorded before. The recordings with Gerald Wilson came afterwards.] But back to the Golden State. You got unhappy with that.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: No, I wasn’t unhappy. I just – one day I said no. I quit that. Just me and music again. Then maybe Dizzy sent for me again.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: ’49. I think ’49.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I went back to New York to stay.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: But what kind of greeting did you get? You took music, right?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah. The guys were cool, but the audience, said, “Girl, (murmur murmur).”

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Really?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Nobody had played no trombone. Nobody.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Yeah. You broke the ice. You were the innovator.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Gerald, he started it. “She wrote the arrangement. She plays, she sings, and all of that stuff.”

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: He did? He told Dizzy that?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: No. He would do that when we were working. Dizzy was the same. He followed up the same way. But the guys were cool.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: It was the other band – was that the ’56 band with Dizzy, where the guys were saying, why’d you send across to the West Coast to get a you-know-what?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah, but, they would do that now. It’s just a man’s thing. They wouldn’t do that to me, but other girls, they would turn up their nose or something.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Dizzy said it was because some of them had friends that they wanted to play, to take that spot, and he sent and got you.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: He said, “Go on and take one of those arrangements out and see if they can play it.” Two or three bars later, he said, “Now who’s the …”

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Yeah, he told me about that, and he relished telling that story, because it confirmed what he felt about – the faith that he had in you.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: He was so good. I was there until the band broke up.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Was that when the work started falling off and Lorraine told him it was the band or her? Is that when the work started falling off for the band.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: It stopped. Not falling off. It stopped. Then I met Randy [Weston] when I was playing with Dizzy, and he said he wanted me to copy or something for him. It turned out that I wrote . . .

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Randy Weston.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Um-hmm. It was a good thing. He took me to Jamaica. He was there visiting his relatives from there, and I was just hanging out.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: I heard how you got the kids to start to read music, to become interested in jazz, and how you got the school systems down there . . .

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I didn’t get the school systems.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Yeah, but what about the . . .

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: The students I got.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Right.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: No sch . . .

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Really? How were you able to [ ? ]

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Because the leaders of the whole island dug me, but the school didn’t.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Really? See, that’s what I wanted to hear too, because you stayed there four or five years, didn’t you?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: No. Five or six years, but when the leaders closed . . .

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Changed.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: . . . I came on out. But I had enough of it.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: You had a lot of kids.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: It was nice. I got a record by one of the students – I’ll tell you tomorrow, I guess.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: I was wondering if you heard from any of your students.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Oh, I hear from them all the time. I’ll play the record for you.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: [asks about Carole Kromer and Diane Gregg who encouraged Liston to come to the Women’s’ Jazz Festival in Kansas City in 1979.]

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: [does not remember their names.] Two women were anxious for her to come to Kansas City.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Were you honored there?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: [cannot remember.]

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: [Did Liston perform there?]

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: [No.]

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: You left there and went to New York, or did you go back to the islands?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I went back to the islands to finish the school, and then I came – I didn’t go to New York. I went to St. Lucia.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Oh. I see the parrot up there. What did you do there?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I had a friend who’s there from [St. Lucia]. He was in Jamaica studying with me and so I went to his hometown and just hung out there for a while.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: You didn’t teach or anything?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: No. They had a symphony orchestra there. [Liston cannot recall details, but she did something with the symphony.] He had his family there.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: You stayed how long?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: It was two weeks or so.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: And then you came back to New York?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: To New York. Um-hmm. I had all my stuff sent back there while I was in St. Lucia.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: I see. It was there waiting when you got back.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Um-hmm.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: And what did you do at that time. Was that still ’79?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I bought me an apartment and settled down.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Shall we mention the magic word?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: What is that?

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Married.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: [does not recall the date]. He just died a few months ago.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: He was a good guy.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Good and bad and all of that stuff, and I was good and bad and all of that stuff. I guess I was getting ready to leave him a long time, maybe three or four times before I actually left him.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Was he a musician?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: No.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: That’s right. You said none of them were musicians.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Two husbands. One of them didn’t last no time, because he was on some stuff or something, but my husband that I – I loved him.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: That wasn’t hard to say, was it?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: No. But you get tired or something. It don’t matter too much.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: But you said he cared about you and he’d just call to see how you were.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: He cared, and then he didn’t care, and then I left him, and then he started up again.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: He started caring, right? He missed you.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Something like that. He used to come and see me in New York there. When I came out here he used to call me up all the time, and I’m sorry he’s gone.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: When you had your stroke, did he come to see you?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah. He was nice like that. Both of us just decided not to go through with the marriage no more.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: But he didn’t resent your music.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: No. He was glad for my music.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Did he come to see you play?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Oh yeah. Now and then. [Liston recalls an incident in Washington.] We were all tired. I was coming back from somewhere. “We’ll stop in Washington and rest and then go on to New York.” All the guys were downstairs. I was in a room upstairs, and didn’t have no clothes on or nothing. I was just getting ready to doze, and here comes one of the fellows. He took off all of his clothes. “You can’t do that.” I was trying to get him out of the room, and the baby’s mama come, and I couldn’t say nothing. “Get out. Get out. Don’t you ever come.” I don’t know whether she’s alive or not, but her husband’s dead. I told him what happened, but she wouldn’t hear it.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: She wouldn’t believe you?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I didn’t talk to her no more. I tried to. I tried to call her up. I talked to her husband, and I told him. But I think she’s dead now. But anyway, that’s what girls have to go through.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: That’s right. That was the one thing that made me [?], because I know that’s what we went through.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: That’s the only . . .

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: . . . thing you’re divulging. But do we get the name of your husband we were talking about.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah. Nelson Harris. Len Sirrah – that’s the name of one of my tunes is his name backwards. It’s a nice tune too. I’m hoping to do that when I go back to New York.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: So you guys had – you had an apartment. But you guys had an apartment together though, didn’t you, because you were mentioning something about . . .

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I think I had it, and then we got married and he came in on it. Then I left, and he stayed.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: You said he’s deceased now.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah. He was in South Carolina visiting his mom. He died there.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: While you were in New York this time, at the beginning of the ’80s, was that when you started organizing your own group? And what about the group that you had with Boo – Boo Pleasant, when you guys went to – Bermuda?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: We worked and worked all around New York and then we went to China. I don’t know what town now. But we went over there and then we came back and then I started weeding the girls out and putting some men in their places.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: That was after Dizzy’s – somebody’s band broke up and this agent said, “You don’t have to be without work. You take a girl’s group” to wherever, and that’s the way that started.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: [does not recall how long they were together.]

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: But then you did start another group for girls, and then you started adding guys, like Britt Woodman. But first you added, I think, a piano player?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Melba Liston and Company, that was all the time. So whatever my company was, that was it, but it was girls all the way and then I had Larry, I had [?]. I don’t know what happened to . . .

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Saxophone player, right?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Alto. And then Budd Johnson. [Liston cannot recall whom Johnson replaced.] Then I had trombone – Al Grey. He played trombone with me. He’d been everywhere I’ve been. He comes in there once in a while. So we had a tenor, an alto, and two ’bones, and the rhythm. I got rid of the bass, because I wanted a upright bass, and she didn’t . . .

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: What’s her name on bass, that sings too? I can’t think of what her name is.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: But now she’s – I talked to [?Colby], and she’s playing upright.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Upright? Because I never have seen her play upright. We better put her name on here if we’re going to talk about her. Was Jean Davis in that group? Trumpet player.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: No trumpets.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: No trumpet. Just sax and ’bone.
Did you write all the music or did anyone else write?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: [No.]

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: You wrote all the music?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yes.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Did you record any music?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: We did, but they didn’t release it or something like that. I didn’t play you the first song that was on the tape. That was with my small group.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: That she just played from the radio date?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Uh-hmm.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: But I thought that was My Reverie from Dizzy’s . . .

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: No. When she – the very first thing . . .

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Oh, that was just the introduction to it. I see.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: . . . before she talked at all. Because Hale Smith – all of those things was talking about that tune that I did.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Because I’d never heard that before.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I haven’t done anything out here. I came out here when I had the stroke and everything.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: But you were playing up until that time, right?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Um-hmm. I don’t know. I was conducting and stuff more than playing. I didn’t play very much at that time. When I was in Jamaica, I had two horns, but I wasn’t playing them. I just carried them around with me. They had a jazz festival or something like that. This was 1975. They had [Frank Foster]. Dexter came.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Did Al come down – Al Grey?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: No. He didn’t come down there. Just saxophone players. That’s all – telling them more about jazz and bebop and all of that stuff. So it was nice.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Long, tall Dexter. How much time do we have? Because I want to bring up about your movie work.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: That was just something.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: I know, but it was an important something.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: You make too much of these . . .

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: No, I’m not making too much. That’s important.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: [cannot recall how it happened.]

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Was first The Ten Commandments?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah. I was with a whole bunch of people, so that – I couldn’t see me as anything on that. But the next one . . .

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: The Prodigal? Lana Turner?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah. I was all through that. I was her maid or something or other. I don’t see it on t.v. or nothing. I’m looking all the time. I’m looking for it.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Why?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I want to see me.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: You say you were playing the lute or what?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: No. I . . .

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: You following her around playing the harp?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: No. I’m her maid.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Somebody got that wrong then.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yes sir. I was her maid or something. No music. I was all through that one. If they show it and I didn’t know about it, I’ll tell you.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Okay, because I haven’t seen that movie, like you said. I haven’t seen it in a long time. So I’ve forgotten. It was Lana Turner, and I forget the name of . . .

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I was Lana Turner’s old girl.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: You don’t remember how you got it. That was one of the main things that I wanted to find out.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I can’t remember.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: But continuing on with the girl groups in New York – what came after? Did you do some more stuff with Randy?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I’ve been writing for Randy. I’m still writing for Randy. I wrote for him up until I had the stroke. After I had the stroke and got over a little bit, I’m writing for him again. I think he pulled me out of it – helped anyway. I thank him very much for sticking with me, because nobody else did.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: My doctor said you find out who your friends really are.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Oh yeah. My friends really are Frank and all of those. They’re arrangers too. I can’t take nothing away from them. They’ll be my friends.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: There was a bass player that . . .

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Major Holley?

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Yeah, Major Holley. You’re always talking about him. He talked about you the whole time . . .

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: He bought my first – the first computer that I had.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: That’s right, but then someone had stolen it or something – you said stole your trombone?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Um-hmm.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Broke into your apartment and stole your stuff or something? When we were in New York—what? – ’88 or something, he told us that.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: He went with me and picked out my first computer.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: I think you had just bought it then, because he was telling me and Jeannie Cheatham about that.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I had the stroke already. I don’t know if I was talking or not then. But he got me and we went downtown and bought the computer.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Had you ever used one before?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: No.
[end of December 4, 1996, interview session]
[December 5, 1996:]

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Melba, the first thing I want to ask you: who was your main influence on the trombone when you started? Was it somebody you really like?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: No. Tommy Dorsey was – I didn’t know too many trombone players, but he was on the radio, and I listened to him. But other than that, I just loved the instrument. I didn’t need no inspiration.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: A lot of your arrangements, are they Ellington-inspired? I get some nuances in some of your stuff, the way you lay it out. Do you like Ellington’s arrangements.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I loved them, but I don’t have anybody – I do it all from my soul, and if it sounds like somebody, well it sounds like somebody. It’s my inspiration. It’s from my soul.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: When you write for your group, is it more swing-oriented or bebop? – when you had your group, like your ’Bones, Melba and her ’Bones, and Friends.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Melba and Friends or Melba and Company. I don’t know. Swing or something.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: But did you ever write “outside,” so to speak?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: No. Not for my group. No. I don’t think so, but maybe somebody else thinks differently. I don’t know. But I don’t think so.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: But do you like “outside” music?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: No. I don’t think so. It’s got to be way “outside.”

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Have you encountered any problems with the bands and the musicians that you have written for in regards to the way you write for the reeds or trumpets?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah. A little bit, but three or four bars in they’d start over again, and everything’s cool. Not recently or in the last 20 years or something, but before then I think there was some kind of animosity until they got into my arrangements, and they’d say “oo” and they’d start it over again.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: It’s like teaching an old dog new trick. How was it when you wrote with Oliver Nelson? He’s a hell of an arranger too.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: What?

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: No problems there? He loved your writing too?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah, and I loved his.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: No problems.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: No, not with nobody. Arrangers, we all friends. Ernie Wilkins and all of us real close. I write the soul music, more or less, and they write the swing and bop stuff.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: What about [Thelonious] Monk?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Right there for me all the time. What about him? I don’t know nothing about him.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Did you ever play any of his music? Did you ever play with him?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: No.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Did he ever play any of your music?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah, I wrote for him, but I didn’t write no different. I just wrote from my soul. I just write what I write. If they like it, they like it. If they don’t . . .

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: But he liked it.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah. They really don’t ask me to do nothing “outside.” It’s always something like a original or one of their tunes, and it’s a great honor – Monk.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: What about Diana Ross? How was she? That was at Motown?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: [cannot recall.]

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: How was that? How was she to work with?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I guess okay. I didn’t have no problem ever. Not with the singers and the instrumentalists that I wrote for. Maybe a bandperson now and then, but he would come in right quick. Not in the last 20 years. I haven’t had none of that.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: What about Abbey Lincoln?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Oh, she’s fine. I write for her now and then.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: John [?]. All that music over there.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I wrote for him. I haven’t written for him since I had the stroke and all of that. I called him on the phone, but I couldn’t reach him up there, outside of New York. I can’t think of it now. He’s – it’s always fine. He lost a boy in that big thing, the airplane crash.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: She did? The same one that what’s-his-name’s wife – Wayne Shorter?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Um-hmm. That was when I was trying to call him, but I didn’t reach him.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: But tell me about you and [Charles] Mingus. Tell me something exciting, because you know I know how Mingus is.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Not with me.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: I don’t mean that way, but I mean I know how he is about his music.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: That’s what I mean. I don’t know nothing about that other thing. Mingus was all music with me, but I haven’t written for him in such a long, long time I can’t even remember how he was or anything. He was all right

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: But you knew him out here?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah. That was a long time ago. He did all his writing. Maybe one or two things I wrote for, but not many things. Watson: How was writing for Mingus different than it was writing for Monk?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: All the world difference. Monk is Monk and Mingus is Mingus. They’re too many things apart. Monk is a piano player and he does things with the piano that nobody else does, and I have to leave spaces and stuff for him. Mingus. It’s altogether different for Mingus. Either you do or you don’t for Mingus. I can’t remember anything
negative about him. I write something and then I leave holes and stuff for him and then write something else to take it out, for Mingus. Watson: What was most challenging about writing for Mingus?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I write for everybody, and they’re all challenging. Anybody I write for, because I haven’t had no training, so I have to dig down and do it from there. All my things are challenging.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: What are some of the challenges that you’ve found when you write for different people? Do they tell you what they want and lay it out, and then you go from there, from what you feel about that, or do you have to really think, like you said, and know the person and write from what you’ve got inside?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Some people, they ask for this and that and the other, and you have to write for them like a stage act, but mostly I write for bands, and they tell me go ahead, do whatever you want to do. Sometimes I’m writing for bands that have criteria and then sometimes I’m free to write. Randy, I have all the freedom I want.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: What’s the criteria for writing for him then? Just whatever you feel? He gives you the song or the changes?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah, he gives me the song and the changes, and that’s all. But we’ve been together – what? – ’56 to ’96. How many is that? 40 years. He don’t tell me anything.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Because you probably already know before he says it, after 40 years.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: He says I write like he writes.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: There’s no challenge there. It is a challenge, but . . .

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Not in the way that people think. I think about it and think about it and think about it before I write. I was writing, before my eyes got bad, a thing for the trumpet player and trombone player that sent me the horn, because I’ve got to send them something, so I was writing for them. Every time . . .

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: You mean Susan? Susan Slaughter?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: . . . Yeah – I go back over it, I’d change it. I tell you why. I’ll be through with it one of these days.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Before the next conference.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah. The trumpet and the trombone and strings.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: What? She sent you a layout for it and then you . . .?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: No, no, no. She don’t even know about it. I just want to do that, because she was sending me the horn, so I got to send her something, so I’m sending her one of my compositions.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Maybe they’ll perform it at the conference.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I don’t know. Maybe. Don’t ever . . .

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: I won’t say anything, but that is great.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Just strings and trumpet and trombone. That’s the first I’ve written for that. I’ve written for trumpet and strings. I hadn’t written for trombone and strings before.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: You’re really reaching down.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: You’ve got to reach down on everything. I have to anywhere. I don’t know where to go until I reach down and find something.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: What you come up with is good, all good. How did you meet Randy? Was he playing – was it out here or in New York when you met Randy?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I was playing with Dizzy – I guess Birdland. I came out and did my usual thing. He stayed over and met me when I finished the gig. He said, “I have to meet her.” We just hit it off right away.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Had you heard of him?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Oh yeah. I hear of everybody. I didn’t expect to see him or to write for him or anything like that. He said, “Can I bring some lead sheets up to your house and you make them for me?” I said okay. He brought Little Niles and all those things up to the house, and he said, “I think you should write these things for an album for me.” And I wrote them. I think it’s the best thing. Quite nice. It’s the best thing. I’m on it. Johnny Griffin, and Ray Copeland. And he and probably Charli Persip – can’t think of the bass player now. It’s a nice album.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: I haven’t heard it in so long. Did they re-release it?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Not yet. But they will. [Randy’s newer things have been reissued.]

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Then that’s the way it started, and it’s gone on 40 years. There’s an awful lot of CDs over there. How many of them did you write?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: All of them, except the ones that he had playing with the rhythm or one horn, but all the things with three horns or more, I wrote. The albums that I used to – there’s a whole bunch of them in my collection over there.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Before CDs?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah. I don’t know what to do with them. I’m going to keep them. That’s all I can do.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: I hope you do. It’s your writing.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I’ve got a bunch of things. Johnny Griffin and all the things I wrote before CDs – I mean, before that.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Before 33 and 1/3.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah I think so.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: I think that Basie thing was on a 78. When you go to New York, will you be writing with Randy?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah. He’s looking forward to my coming there, but so many others are waiting for me to come there too, to write or . . .

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: That was obvious at the rehearsals for the Groove Festival. They would be waiting for you. Does Charli Persip want you to write for his big band?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: When you get to New York, do you have any future plans?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Colby, she going to be my – so we’re talking once a week or so now. She’s got everything going, but I told her, Randy and then other things, because he – Randy pulled me out of the stroke, so I have to go with him.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Because you used to say, whenever you would be sad or something, you’re horn would bring you out of it, but now you can’t depend on that, so Randy is your horn right now. Have you fulfilled all your dreams and goals and stuff for yourself, or did you have any new come along? You’ve written for everybody. You played with everybody.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I haven’t mad no money. So I could make some money now.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: That’s probably what you’ll do, going back to New York. Like you said, they’ll be ready for you, and they won’t be piddly-paddling with the money.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I don’t like the music today, the music that the youngsters are doing today. I’m an old-fashioned broad, and I just want to do other . . .

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: You don’t like rap?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: It’s okay.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Fusion?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: What is the fusion?

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Fusion is where they mix the – they try to mix bop and rock-and-roll . . .

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: No. I don’t think so. I wouldn’t say. That’s all right. It’s that other thing.
[Liston fails to identify the style she has in mind.]

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Melba, do you think that the kids are not – nowadays with their music, the direction they are going, that there is a – it’s blah. It’s not – as far as I’m concerned, there’s no soul there. There’s no meat, no bottom. What do you think?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: It’s nothing there. Once in a while a person comes along and has the business and soul and everything, but ordinarily, youngsters don’t have nothing.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Do you think it’s because they didn’t have like what we had when we came – we had places to go and listen and have the older people walk you through to where you – do you think that’s missing? They don’t have a common place to go, like we used to.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I don’t think so. They wouldn’t take it. They just want to do their thing, and I guess maybe they’ll come out of it and go into something nice maybe 10 years or something, but nothing there – I don’t hear nothing in the way they’re doing it nowadays.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: But people like – we heard David Sanchez. He reached back to a lot of guys from Bird on up. A little of Ben Webster. But you’re not saying that they have to be imitating or using – that’s not what you’re saying.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: No. They just have to have some soul. That’s all.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: How are they going to get it.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I don’t know. They have it or you don’t have it. Watson: Do you think that the fact that many of the young musicians coming up today have not had the experience of playing in big bands has contributed to the fact that – do you think that the experience of playing in a big band gave you anything that they’re lacking by playing only in small-group performance?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: No, because they could have it solo-wise, if they had it at all. I don’t know what it is that they’re lacking, but I’m not well-schooled in the youngsters and everything any more.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: But don’t you think that these colleges – they have the big bands and they have the workshops. The Berklee School of Music. They’re turning them out. But there’s still something missing.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Once in a while, one cat will – somebody came up with some school in the midwest. They were all white kids except one black boy, and he said, the black boy was the only one that had some soul in the whole school.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Why? Different background?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Maybe they just got it and others don’t have it and won’t have it.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: But you don’t think that by not coming out with the big bands, because you came in on the tail end of the big bands.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I was there for a whole – I guess it was a long time. But Dexter and all of those people, they were going around soloing, piano and bass and stuff, and soloing, and they had it.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: I wanted to ask you about Dexter. What did you think about his playing?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Oh, dear me. Everything good.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: He played like he walked. You went to school with him, right?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah, junior high school. He came down to Jamaica when I was down there teaching and played for the kids. [Liston tries to recall the name of a drummer who was also there.] He had a band then and he had a band now, and he’s married to a Japanese – Elvin Jones. Elvin came down with his group. I can’t say all the musicians that came down – once in a while – and played for my kids and the school, and some of those got soul. It’s nothing I can put my finger on. I don’t know what it is.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: I wanted to ask you about those schools in New York that you – you helped to start a couple of schools. You helped establish the Pittsburgh Jazz Orchestra in Pennsylvania in 1964, and then you – the Harlem Backstreet Tour Orchestra. I’d never heard of these. The Pratt Institute Youth in Action. Do you remember those pretty good groups? You wrote music for them, or you rehearsed them? – in the ’60s.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I wrote and I directed. Maybe sometimes they were just coming along with their instruments. They weren’t about getting no arrangement and stuff. They were just starting on their instruments, so I would help them out with chords and scales and stuff like that. I was in Pittsburgh and Washington. [Liston points to (?a photograph) in the room.] I did a lot for them in Philadelphia and the person that was getting the students together, he came down to Jamaica and he was there when they took my picture. It was two, three years I went back and forth to Philly to do church things.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: What about the film, The Marijuana Affair?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: [cannot recall details.]

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: How did the record date come up with Melba and her ’Bones. On your first one you had Bennie Green, Al Grey, Benny Powell.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: No, I had girls first.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Really? I mean the record date, I mean. I’m speaking of.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I know, but I had the girls first, and we went all over the East Coast, and we went to China and came back.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Is that the one with Bu?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Um-hmm. And I started weeding them out, one-by-one. I don’t remember who was trying to get us a record date. But anyway, we got some records, but they didn’t put them out, but they had them.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Oh really?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: So I don’t think – oh, Leonard Feather. That’s who that – yeah, he was still around.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: He always likes to dabble with the women. But he didn’t put them out.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: He was the one that got me the record date, but the record company was . . .

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Were you satisfied with the record?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: No. Not – some of them. Some of the tunes. Some of them I didn’t – I had to do one of his things.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Oh, yeah. You always have to do that.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: And one or two pop things or something, and I didn’t – I don’t know how I did them, but it was just me, and I don’t like them today. I don’t know if the tempos are wrong or something. I don’t know what. But anyway.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: That’s with the all girls.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: No. I had them all changed about now.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: But you had two separate ’bone sections on two different record dates. One was around Christmas time – they both were around Christmas time – one around the 22nd, one around the 24th. One you had Slide Hampton, Frank Rehak.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Oh. That was a different Company altogether. I forgot about that. And Randy, we had a date with him and the 4 ’bones too. I’ll play it for you when we get finished with this.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Before we go to the music, I wanted to ask you, does it strike you funny, with all your experiences and your writing, technique, and expertise in doing so many – on your horn and everything – does it strike you funny or kind of sad that a large record company has never signed you to a contract? Do you think it’s because of the gender or something?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I’m a woman. That’s that. I don’t know. I don’t have a manager that pushes me out there and all of that.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: You never had a manager?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Colby. That’s all.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: I meant . . .

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Nobody.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: That is one of the problems.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: But maybe it was good, because I wouldn’t – I don’t know if I was ready for that.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: When you were travelling on a State [Department] tour, where all – Middle East, right? You went to the Middle East and you went to South America, where some the dates in the Middle East, I think I read where you said that the women were amazed that you could be up there doing what you were doing, and they weren’t allowed the freedom. How did the people – did you get more acceptance than anybody else in the band?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Almost everywhere I got acceptance. My applause and everything was always great, over there and here and everywhere, but some places – I don’t know where – but some places women weren’t allowed to do nothing but cook and I don’t know. But I’m from the States. I’m always accepted, even though their women weren’t allowed to.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Did the women ever talk to you about that?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: No. I didn’t have – I didn’t talk to – I was talking about music. I didn’t talk to no women, nothing about no home life and all of that stuff. I didn’t even know about it. That was a shame, because I should have talked to them.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Could have gotten a different insight.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I don’t know about that, but I should have talked to them.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: But do you think your reception was greater in other parts of the world?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Oh yeah. Everywhere except here, the United States.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Especially as far as jazz is concerned?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah. I think classical or anything, more accepted, more Europe and the Middle and South America than here. I don’t know what it is about this. Maybe I’m not attuned to – I don’t know what it is.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: What about China?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: That was nice to us. They took us around and showed us everything and bought us a lot of things to send home for our . . .

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Souvenirs?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah. It was a nice trip.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: The reception was very good.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Did you find that they knew more about you and the guys than the people here in the States?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I don’t know. I should have talked to them. I don’t know if they knew or if I was a surprise or anything. I don’t know. But the heads of state or something knew we were coming. I don’t know about the masses. I don’t know.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: But it’s been said over there, at the State Department – on a State Department tour, that your arrangement on My Reverie – no, Anitra’s Dance – Annie’s Dance would break the ice, because there was – they recognized the theme and they liked your arrangement – treatment of it. Is that true?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Dizzy and you had to play politics?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I don’t know if – I was just doing whatever . . .

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: He told me

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: . . . and he was just doing whatever. We weren’t no – I wasn’t doing any politics.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: I know. I know you weren’t.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Dizzy, I guess, was doing it, but we didn’t see it. I didn’t know that Dizzy was doing everything that he was doing to keep us together and all that.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: What kind of – you wrote a compilation of music for this tour that included excerpts from Duke and Basie and all those people. You know what I’m speaking of? You put that together? You put – you remember that?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I can remember somebody saying, “Do this,” but it was nothing. I mean, I played with all of them, so it was nothing for me to take a little bit of this and a little bit of that.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: But I think this was – they were saying that you were asked to do this for that tour.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah, but I didn’t – it was nothing for me to do it.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Right, because you had played with them. Right?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah, or else I had listened to them all the time. I was the one – all the other guys – Ernie and – were there.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Was Benny Golson there?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah. And they chose me to do that, because I guess I listened to them all the time. But I can’t remember. I did whatever they told me, and that was one of the things that they told me, and it was just another job for me to do. That’s all.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: When you guys did the South American tour, did you do Cuba at that time?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: No.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Did you ever go to Cuba with Dizzy?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: No, I don’t think so. I got some work, but we weren’t together.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Where did you go in South America?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: South of there. Not Cuba.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: That was Wynton Kelly and that group? Ernie Henry. You did a record with Ernie Henry, right? Good alto player.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah. Wynton’s a fine pianist. Oh dear. I think we were – I was supposed to marry him, but he died over there in Canada or somewhere.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Yeah, he was a nice person. Last time I saw him he was pianist for Dinah Washington. Oh yeah – how was that? How was Dinah to work with? She gave you no problems.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: No. Everybody – no problems. Nobody.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: You wouldn’t stand for it? Is that it?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: No. Nobody gave me no problems. I didn’t have no problems, because they didn’t give me no problems. If they gave somebody else a problem, I didn’t know about it. They were saying, Ray Charles, turn off the lights and give this woman a fit and all that. I said, no. We were together – I worked for him for two or three years, and I . . .

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: They were good experiences.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: He was just always nice. So I don’t know about these other things.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Attitude and all.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah. I don’t know about those, because they didn’t show me that.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: They had a lot of respect for you then.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I guess so.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: I’ve seen Ray and Dinah go off on people for no reason. You’re better at music. You didn’t have that problem.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: No.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: You wrote for Sam Jones.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: [can’t recall.]

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: We’re going to change the format here a little bit, Melba, and do – let’s hear some music, some of your arrangements, and we’re going to comment on it. First thing I want to hear, Austin Cromer sings your arrangement of If You Could See Me Now. That was great. [The music plays.] How did you write that arrangement, Melba? Oh man, and sit through them playing it like that? Isn’t that a thrill? Do you get thrilled when you hear your arrangements?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Sometimes.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Just sometimes? This should have been one of the times.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I watch you getting thrilled, and then I get a thrill from that.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Because after you guys had done that, now who was it that came over and I played this and your Reverie and Annie’s Dance and everything, and you should have seen the expressions on the whole – I’m trying to think who it was that they were – that came over. I was always there with somebody – somebody out of Basie’s band, and we were playing that music. That was beautiful. What gave you the – who suggested that tune?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I guess he did. I wrote it. I don’t know. I don’t think Dizzy had anything to do with it.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: But you two got together. When you were getting it together, do you go to the piano?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I used to. Yeah. Now it’s that electric thing over there.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: The keyboard.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: But I used to.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: But anyway, there’s a keyboard involved. Who was the bass player? Was that Paul [West]?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I think so. Maybe it was . . .

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: He was in and out of that thing.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I forget.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Because I like the bass player too. But I liked the way you do your shadings. The trumpets blare out and you drop it down and the reeds are under, and then the trumpets are – that’s – to me that’s kind of a lost art in arrangement.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I guess so.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: You haven’t noticed that?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I still write like that.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: I know, but you haven’t noticed that other people have lost that art? The shadings.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I don’t know of anybody that’s doing that, but I don’t hear Benny Golson’s and Randy – I mean Ernie’s – I don’t hear those things, so I don’t know whether they’re doing that or not.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: But did you use that with your colleagues – your bands down in Jamaica? Did you – you taught them about shadings and . . .

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Oh, yeah. But that was the very end. I was busy trying to lay – tell them what the notes were and all of that. But they got it.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: But doesn’t that go back to when Mrs. Hightower was teaching you – I know she taught you. That’s an old-school type thing. You had to have – you start off high, where you going to go? That was one of my teacher’s favorite sayings. You can’t start at the top of the tower . . .

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: And go anywhere. No, you have to start from scratch.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: And when you’re directing your tunes, you make sure that – you notate that on your arrangements, right? When you’re writing, have you had a problem with drummers doing the shadings and things?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: No so much. I would tell them – I wouldn’t . . .

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Notate it?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: The parts – I wouldn’t note it on the parts, but I would tell them.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: In your directions?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah, and they were good.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Charli [Persip] seemed to have been well versed in that. He knew a lot – shading and dynamics and things like that. That was in the ’50s. We’re going to do another thing from that same album. We’re doing – You’ll Be Sorry – this one’s going to feature Melba, singing and writing it and arranging it. [The music plays.]
Who decided that?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I don’t know. I did. I don’t know. I wrote it, so I decided it.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: But I mean for this record date, who decided they would put it on the record date?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Dizzy, I guess all the tunes.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: But you had been doing this with the band?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Did you do it over – undoubtedly over in the Far East.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Um-hmm.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Oh, great. That’s a cute little tune. And boy, you had your wind power there. You get a long stretch without a breath there. I kept waiting for you to breathe.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I used to – no problem there, when I was young.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: And then one phrase there you really sounded like Billie Holiday.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Oh yeah?

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: During the first part of it. [Bryant sings the melody quietly.] I’m trying to think of it. I think it’s around the fourth bar of the first 8. It’s some word, and your nuance was strictly Billie and you had that kind of little – Billie had a way kind of like [Bryant vocalizes] – yeah, you had that. You have that. But that arrangement, you – your – those things you have – the fill-ins behind the phrases of the words and then behind Dizzy when he’s playing, that’s perfect. Just beautiful.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Thank you.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Did it take you long to write that down?
