items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I don’t think so.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Because you were writing for you.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: It was – when I was writing, I was writing those in matter of days. I can’t write like that no more.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: That’s good then. That was good. So we’ve seen two sides of you. Now we’re going to see another side of your writing. We’re going to try another one of Melba’s arrangements with Dizzy’s band, a little something different. It’s – she calls it Annie’s Dance, and it’s a play on the semi-classical tune called Anitra’s Dance. [The music plays.] That is really a beautiful arrangement on that.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: It’s still good.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Yes, it’s still good. The interplay between the sections, and when Charli Persip with his – he sounds like somebody tiptoeing on the drums, tap-dancing or something. Your shadings and everything.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah, that’s good.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Did you write – you wrote that before you guys went over, right?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Oh yeah. We were at Birdland.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: That’s where you tried it out? You tried it out at Birdland?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I didn’t try out.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: No, what I mean, you try something out before you go over . . .

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: No.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: You played it. I mean you played it.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: We were . . .

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Working there.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: . . . working there, wherever we were, before – we didn’t know about . . .

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Birdland? The tour?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: . . . when I wrote it.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Oh. Okay.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Some things you just – you got to write some things. So he told me to write some things, so I . . .

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: That’s one of the things you wrote.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: That’s – we’ve heard three different styles of your writing, because everybody refers to you as a ballad-type person, melodic and all that stuff, but you’ve thrown in the blues, and then you’ve thrown in this production.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I thank you.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: I wanted you to talk about how you put it together, whatever, when you were putting it together.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I can’t remember. The same as I do now. You sit and think about it and think about it and then you start writing it. My ’bones – I have interplay with the ’bones, but saxophones – the trumpets too. They have interplay. Maybe two of them play and then two of them play after that. Something like that. I don’t know. But it’s not a planned thing. It’s just a thing that . . .

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: It’s just what you hear.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: . . . you happen to go on with where the arrangement goes, and you say, oh, this one will go right.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: When you’re writing, do you write your arrangements like down straight through, or do you write this and hear something else down the line and write that in?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I write almost straight through and then I go over it and then no telling what happens. Like this one I’m writing now. I’ve gone over it two or three times, and then each time I said, no, and I change it. I don’t know. It’s just . . .

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: You edit a lot.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: That’s the word.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: When you edit it down, boy, it’s together. Whatever you take out, I don’t think it belongs in there. Whatever you leave in, it goes. Because I like the way the accents –

like when Billy Mitchell came in on that saxophone, you had set it up. He came in, and Dizzy. Whew. He came in. And I noticed that the drums accent with the trumpet. Do you do that a lot? Do you write for the drums too?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: I noticed on that arrangement, that he catches all of those licks

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Okay, we’re going to move on, and is this Little Niles? Watson: My Reverie.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Oh yeah, My Reverie. Oh yeah, Melba, My Reverie. The first time I heard that – wow. That is – honestly, and I’ve told two or three people that, and I’m getting goose bumps just thinking about – that is one of the most beautiful things you’ve ever done – especially the haunting sound that you get on your trombone and what you write behind what you’re doing. Let’s listen – hear what I’m trying to say. [The music plays.] Hey that’s so pretty it makes you want to cry, Melba. And you know you used that [wah-wah sound], and you know where Dizzy uses the last time he played on record, on that record he did with kids up in ’Frisco? What are they called? And the last – on his favorite song that I love – He wrote the song. And he used to – when I’d go up to the club, he’d stop the band. They’d play this song. I Waited for You. Remember he did that on the end of that? I think he must have been thinking about Melba, because I – that set the whole thing for me. What were you thinking about when you . . .

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I don’t know.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Yes you do. You have to. When you are playing something like that, Melba, or you’re writing something, you’ve got to have – you’ve got to – either your old man was something or other.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: No

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Come on.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: No.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: You just wrote that off the top of your head like that and played that like that?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I played whatever . . .

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Came in your mind?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah. That particular time. I don’t know if I played it the next time like that or not.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: That’s what I’m saying.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: So I don’t know. But it wasn’t about nothing.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: No? Melba, you can ’fess up.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: About nothing – about the notes. That’s about the notes. That’s about the notes. That’s all.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Anybody plays like that, got to be thinking about something. Melba?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I got to be thinking about the notes, man. I got to be thinking about the notes – the notes, man.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: And the arrangement – you set yourself up so good.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Maybe I was arranging, I thought about something. I don’t know. But blowing, I don’t think about nothing but the notes.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Is that right?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: That one, anyway.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Okay, clean it up, Melba. And I’ve heard guys say that when they’re playing, like a ballad, they’re usually thinking about some situation or some woman or something that really makes them put a little more oomph into it, a little more edge, a little more soul. I mean, with some of those notes you were playing on there, especially on the tag – you know when you’re going out, and you kept going up [Bryant sings the trombone melody.] Something was goosing you.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I don’t know. I don’t know what it was.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Okay. I’m trying to get it out.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I don’t really – I’m just thinking about the notes. I mean, really.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Okay. Okay. All right. Well, you’re one in a million.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Oh, boy. If I could do that that now.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Yeah. Wouldn’t that be something?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yes indeed.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Don’t you miss it?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I’m going to blow it two or three years from now, I guess, or something, but I’m going to blow it.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Okay. That’s a promise?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah, that’s a promise.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Because I want to hear you again Melba.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I’m blowing it every now and then, but I can’t get but two or three notes on the thing.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Those two or three notes, you can take them and do something magical with them.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah, but I got to – I have this arm. I don’t know what to do with this. I tried to turn the thing around and blow it like Slide Hampton, and I can’t . . .

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: You can’t do nothing.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: No, man. The thing comes off. It just – I can’t do nothing. Oh, man. So I had to turn it back around, because I don’t want to . . .

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Is this the hand you hold it with or slide it?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: No. Sliding.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Oh, man. Are you exercising it every day?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Oh yeah.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: You’re doing more than you were doing.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: But I don’t know – I think I’m doing . . .

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: You are doing more than you were doing. I know you are. Definitely.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah, so maybe . . .

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: In less than in two years. Coming up right now, we’re going to do one of Randy Weston’s tunes, a song that was recorded for the first time I think in 1956. It’s called Little Niles, and it’s Melba Liston’s arrangement of it, and this is another one of the styles and different ways that Melba writes. We want to hear this. Little Niles. [The music plays.] I like the way the bass comes in.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah, that was featuring the bass.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: And the – it had a flavor of . . .

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Of Monk?

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Yes.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Randy likes Thelonious much.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: He does [Bryant vocalizes].

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah. He does that.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: I don’t get to hear Randy’s work that often. That a 1956 version of that.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah. You want to go on and hear [?] or this one – the strings?

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Oh yeah, because I haven’t heard you do strings arrangement.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Or else I can do the one that I’m featured on.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Yeah. You said that was next.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I think it was next.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Can you cue that up for us? But you were on this one too.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah, but I didn’t know. I forgot. The other one is more ballad and it’s easier.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: You don’t know the name of it.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: [cannot recall.] I think it’s the next one on the box there.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: This is another one of Randy Weston’s tunes. It features Melba on this one, and we’ve searched and searched, and we can’t find the title of it, but maybe later on we can cue Matt as to what it is, and he can put it – fill it in, but let’s hear – I think it’s a ballad. [The music plays.]

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: [while the music plays] So that – don’t stop it, but that’s about all that I can say, that I’m featured on it. That little bit. But it’s nice.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: That was – he seems to 3/4 time or 6/8 time.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah, 3/4. All the waltz – that album was all 3/4.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Oh, okay. You kind of wove in and out of the [?]. It was – [Bryant hums to herself] I’m trying to think. It reminds me of something. That’s your arrangement?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: You always thinking who or where or something.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Yeah, I do. I really do, because I’ve been – I get programmed like that from the radio shows that they usually mess up, so I start thinking ahead of them. But anyway, this one, we don’t have a name to, but do you know how your solo – was it – because it didn’t feature Ray. It was – was it written with you in mind?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah. I wrote it.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Oh, okay. Because that was a beautiful solo, Melba.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Thank you. I was – we were in Baltimore – no, Canada. What’s the name of the town?

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Montreal.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah, Montreal. I wrote it here in L.A., and I did some things outside of New York. I can’t think, but the record was done in Montreal and they were all Montreal strings, but Randy and bass and drums are from New York. Paul . . .

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Who was that?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: The conductor. He was conducting. He was playing bass on the records that – with Dizzy he was playing bass, but on . . .

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Paul West, you mean?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah, but on that he was conducting. He was conducting quite well.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: You wrote this in a different style. It is Little Niles, but it has a classical flavor. You think so? It sounds great.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I don’t know.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Let’s listen to it and see what you think, 40 years later.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: But it’s not that much different. It’s the same thing as far as I’m concerned.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: But strings – to me that makes a difference. [Little Niles plays, in a version for strings and jazz combo.] That was beautiful.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Randy tells me how many choruses he’s going to take and where violins come in, but nothing else.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: That’s all he tells you?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Um-hmm.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: You sure knew what to do. And your voicings on those strings. That’s beautiful. It’s the first time I heard you write for strings, Melba. That’s beautiful. And I’ve heard a lot of people try to write for strings, and it doesn’t have that kind of sound.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: You heard Gloria Lynne?

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: She had strings on it too? I’ve heard it. Is that later – a late one too?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: No, it was way back there.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: I don’t hear it.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: It’s not up there. It’s over here in the . . .

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: That treatment of Little Niles is very unique. It’s different and it’s good. It’s bad. It’s bad, Melba. Very good. I like that. I’ve never it heard it done like that.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I didn’t hear anything different than . . .

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: You have to.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: The horn parts and the string parts are the same. The horns played what the strings are playing there.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: But wasn’t most of that just the rhythm and strings, on this?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: No.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: On the other version . . .

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: But I had horns, and they are playing the same thing as the strings are on this thing.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: I see what you’re saying. On the other record the horns are playing what the strings are playing on this. I get that. But it’s just the sound, and like you say, the voicing was the same on the horns, but the voicing on the strings made it a completely different thing, to me. The last version of Randy Weston’s Little Niles that we just heard, with strings, was from a new CD that hasn’t been released yet. It’s called Earth Birth, and of course the arrangement was by Melba Liston and the strings were out of sight. Wasn’t that beautiful. Okay. We going to jump back in time and hear another version of Little Niles by Randy in Melba’s arrangement. We’re going back to a 1973 version from a CD called Tanjah. Melba, you want to say anything about this before we start?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: No. I’ll say it afterwards. [The music plays.]

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: That’s what you call percussion for days. Yeah, that is a different version.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Today they could program it much better than it was on that, but you could hear it, but if they were to do it now . . .

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: You mean they would re-mix it a little different?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah. That would be . . .

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: It had that Indian – East Indian flavor to me, with a little African thrown in some of the phrases that you had there. And then, what was that on top? A piccolo?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: No.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Or a whistle? Way up there.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: It was . . .

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Fife?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: It wasn’t none of those things.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Okay. At first I thought it was a trumpet. Somebody’s screaming up there. Jon Faddis or somebody.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: It was a mouthpiece.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Oh really?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I think so.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: But that was – how many versions have we heard of it? Four? Heard today?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Three. Wasn’t it three?

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: We heard the original, and the strings, and this one, and they’re all completely different. You arranged all of them.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Not quite different.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: To me, they’re different.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I think there’s some more, but I won’t mention those. I can’t remember where they were anyway, so we’ll go on to . . .

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: But he – but Randy uses his song Little Niles in all these different versions kind of like Dizzy used Manteca and like you did. He changes it up, but it’s still the same song, in different clothing. And that’s great.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: But Pam’s Waltz and Little Niles, he goes – every time he record, we’ll do those things. So anyway . . .

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Yeah. All right, then. That’s what a lot of people do. That keeps the money rolling in too.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Oh yeah.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: You’re getting royalties and all – air play and stuff. That’s great. So that was 1973. Fantastic. Right now we’re going to a little bit more of comparing two of Randy’s tunes at different eras to – this first one we’re going to play would be – is that 1973? – and the tune is called Hi-Fly – h, i, fly. And then we’re going to listen to – just an excerpt of that – then we’re going to listen to the 1996 version of Hi-Fly with Melba’s arrangement, on a new CD that’s not out yet. It’s called Earth Birth. Right now it’s 1973 again. [The music plays, during which Bryant queries the identity of the trumpeter whose solo follows the statement of the theme.]

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: [does not recall.] Okay. You can stop it now. [A slow version of Hi-Fly commences.]

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: I never heard it done like that. It’s beautiful, with the strings and everything, and then I see Randy likes fourths and seconds. I do too. You write a lot of [?] fourths in the harmony, but that – I like the way you wove in and out with the strings – that’s the last one, but Randy was doing so much stuff with the – I mean he was creating so much stuff, but the strings is really a completely huge dimension to your writing that I’d never heard before, Melba. How long have you been writing? This is ’76? No, this is ’96.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah, but I’ve been writing for strings as long as I’ve been – not as long, but once a year . . .

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Gloria?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Gloria Lynne’s thing.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: And that was ’59.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: So I’ve been writing for strings as long as I’ve been writing for horns.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: I heard it. I just didn’t know that was you writing it then.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah. I guess not.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: But that Hi-Fly version – see, that’s two completely different versions of Hi- Fly. One’s with all that Latin – with all that rhythm, and it sounds like Eastern here and then African rhythms in there, and then we come up with the strings and the beauty, and then he gets raunchy a little bit. How did he tell you to do with this one? He said to you, “I’m going to solo so many choruses.”

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: He doesn’t say nothing about the soloing and all that. He wanted it long, and he said, “This chorus I’ll take by myself. This chorus you can do some backgrounds or something.”

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Okay. You guys are so in tune to each other, you don’t need – he doesn’t have to tell you anything anyway.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I don’t think so.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: That’s like the [?]. That’s understood. He doesn’t have to spell it out. But that’s really unique, that version of it, and that’s from the – that one is from the new album, right? Earth Birth. And the one we heard before was from Tanyah, and that was 1973. Now we’re going to hear something else from . . .

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: No. Let’s leave Randy alone now and listen to Gloria Lynne’s Hi-Fly.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: What we’re going to hear now is one of Melba’s original tunes, a beautiful ballad that she did – Gloria Lynne sang it in 1959. The title of the ballad is Love, I Found You. I or I’ve?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I’ve.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: I’ve Found You. And it’s strings. It’s beautiful. Just give it a listen. [The music plays.] That’s beautiful. Love, I’ve Found You. I won’t even go there. But Melba, do you find it different to write for voice and for – with strings, or just regular instruments – just for band with strings?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah. I guess so. Not really, but really.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: But you do have to think a little about it.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: A high voice or a low voice or a in-between voice and all of those things, but then you just go on and write.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Dig deep down and write. That’s a beautiful tune, Melba.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Thank you.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Did you do an album with strings with Dinah [Washington]? What did you do with Dinah?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: [cannot recall. She does not have the recordings.]

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: That flavor of your writing for strings sounds like something I’ve heard on one of her albums, and you have written for Dinah. What – Gloria approached you about writing?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah, and I was sick, and the day of the recording date, I was out of it, so I called Quincy [Jones] and he conducted for me, but all of the arrangements are mine – almost all of them.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Okay. That was 1959.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: You want to [?] or more of hers?

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: What else is on there? Or did you mean another CD?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: [cannot recall.]

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: We’re discussing Gloria Lynne’s record, and you – he was asking you, how did she come to get the – you said you brought it to her and you taught her some of the songs.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Because that’s what we want to get through first. Then we’ll get into the difference between the two. Okay?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Dinah – soul, soul, soul, but Gloria’s soul too, but it’s a different way. They come after me differently. I don’t know how to say it. When I write for Dinah – uh. And when I write for Gloria – it’s oo. Or something like that.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: That tells the difference right there. Right now we’re going to listen to a tune by Gloria Lynne that Melba wrote – an original tune with strings. It’s called We Never Kissed. Ain’t That a Shame? [Actually We Never Kissed, What a Shame; the music plays.]

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: The difference is who picks what songs. Dinah picks some soul songs. Gloria picks some . . .

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: That’s strictly a ballad.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: . . . ballads. Soulful, but not the way Dinah does. Still, writing for them demands what tunes you are going to write. I would write the same way for Gloria Lynne – if I wrote for Dinah – one of those arrangements for Dinah, I would write the same way for Gloria Lynne, but she would sing it differently.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Would interpret. Their interpretations would be different. I see what you’re saying.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I guess. I don’t know.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: I know they would. Dinah wouldn’t sing that like that.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: No, but I don’t know if Gloria – I’m saying now I would write the same, but I don’t, when I get to the piano or get to writing, it’ll be different. I feel like it’s the song, not the singer, makes the difference.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Yeah, because they’re going to put their own flavor into your arrangement anyway. We have some pictures here that Melba’s going to be looking at, from her childhood, that she’s never seen before. Who do you see on there that you recognize, Melba?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Everybody except the drummer, and I don’t know who the tall saxophonist is, but the rest of them I know. That’s me. Minnie – Minnie [?Moore ?Morris].

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: That’s Prince.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah, there’s Prince.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Prince Harris.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: And Elvira. [Liston cannot recall a trumpeter’s name.]

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: But he was a trumpet player?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Uh-huh. His mother and my mother used to be friends. [They fail to identify another trumpeter in the photo.]

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: [They identify Melba and Buddy Redd.] Elvira – Vi Redd’s brother. Do you know about when this was?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: That was 1930-something?

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Yeah, probably was ’38 maybe? No, ’39 or ’40, maybe, because you came out here in ’37, right?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah. It was ’38 or something like that. [Liston fails to identify another man in the photo.]

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: [asks if it was in a picture studio.]

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: [cannot recall.]

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: [shows Liston a second photograph.]

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: This is Ross Snyder. [Liston tries to identify a second man.] I liked him. Not then. Maybe 15 years later. I can’t remember his name.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: [identifies Lorenzo.] Do you remember how he played trumpet? Because he’s a saxophone player. He’s playing trumpet.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah, I know. I don’t know how he’s playing saxophone, because I know him as a trumpet player.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Really? He’s a darned good saxophone player.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah?

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Yeah. Alice worked with him all the time. Alice Young. Up until he died, she was his piano player.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I didn’t know that. [Liston and Bryant identify, in this photograph, Minnie Hightower, her mother Miss Hightower, Vi Redd, Liston. They fail to identify a man in the photograph. Liston thinks it is Robert Ross, but Bryant pulls out a photo of a different man whom she identifies as Ross.]

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: You know Clifford Burden, right?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Oh yeah. He and Minnie both dead, huh?

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Yeah, that’s who Minnie married.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I know.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Her son – their son, Clifford, Jr., is a preacher now, and he’s the one that had the pictures in that box from Minnie’s ex-husband – widow. [They discuss getting copies made for Liston. In a third photograph they identify South Park, Minnie, Alice, Robert Ross, and Clifford in a pseudo-Hawaiian setting. Bryant implies that Matt Watson is photographing or videotaping this portion of the interview, and she states that she intends to use these three photographs in her own book.] Melba, looking around the walls here and seeing some of the many things – many awards and tributes that people have given you, have you reached the goals that you set? Or did you set any goals for yourself when you were coming up?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: No. I just went on and did whatever they told me to do. But I would like to – I haven’t written for films – just films that doesn’t say anything.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: It’s not political. Just a beautiful film.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah. I would like to do that.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Would you say that would be your heart’s goal right now?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: It doesn’t matter if I do or if I don’t. I think maybe something in New York is waiting on me now.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: When you were coming up, you never said, “I want to be the best” or whatever?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: No.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: You never had that kind of . . .

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: No

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: You just knew that you were going to be the best. You didn’t have to say it, right?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I didn’t know.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Yes you did.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: But I have to be the best that I can do. I don’t know if it’s the best.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: I’ll say for you: you have been the best, Melba. You’ve been a guiding light for a lot of people, including me, and I want to ask you what advice you would have for some of the young girls coming along who are musicians? What advice would you give them?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Study. Go to school and learn everything that you can in school, and don’t stop there. Get what you can out of school, jamming and everything. It’s about learning and about doing. It’s hard now. It’s still hard for girls, but . . .

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: But they still won’t have it as hard as you did.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Oh no.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Was there any particular school that you think that they could go to that would really qualify to do what you said, go and learn, not just . . .

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: [cannot recall any school to recommend.] But wherever they go to school, college and stuff, make them teach you as much as they know how. And go on, like we did at nighttime – go to other places and get some knowledge there.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: And do you think that they should pick someone as their model – not particularly role model, but as a model that they would listen to, like I’ve heard Charli Persip say he went to whatever the college was that he went to, but he finished from the Gillespie University. You know what I’m saying?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah, I would say that. Yes indeed. Get someone that you like to have. Horn players, get someone to take a pattern off of. Everything that’s out there, they can have somebody older to pattern off of . . .

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Yeah, they need someone to latch onto.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: . . . and maybe after so many years of that, you can go and get someone else to . . .

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Yeah, right. Move on up to the modern day, or whatever. Do you find that they’re more – the children and young kids coming up, male and female, on the East Coast, seem to be the ones who reach back in – I mean who reach up and take a role model’s hand and try to pattern themselves at the beginning, until they get where they can walk on their – in their own shoes, and then they still want to
recognize where they came from? Because out here on the West Coast I don’t seem to find that.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I don’t see where that’s happening out here.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: No, I don’t either.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: But East Coast . . .

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: I wonder why that is.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I don’t know, because you know better than me. I don’t get around too much, and I wouldn’t get around if I was able to. I would be back in New York.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: You wouldn’t even be here, Melba.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I would come here on occasions.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: But that bothers me, that the kids – they’re not – you know what. It seems like they think the music starts and ends with them, that they – nobody was here before them, so they don’t have to recognize – I really don’t hear kids doing that.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I don’t know what these kids are doing.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: But those schools that you helped organize and stuff like that, the kids wanted to learn, and they came there to learn, and they did learn, because you guys were teaching them.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah. Back there. In the West Indies, St. Lucia, everywhere but here.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Right. Isn’t that funny? In Japan, in Europe. But it’s so funny that we – on this Coast, we cannot get it together, as far as I can see. And you’re not going to stick around and try and help us get it together.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I’ve been here six, seven years or something. I’m going to go back there and get a new start or something.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: “I’m going to change my way of living. If that ain’t enough, I’m going to change the way I strut my stuff.” Because Melba you’ve really overcome the stroke that you had. I think you’ve made a long stride, bettering yourself to overcome that, and I think when you go back East, you’ll do even greater, because like you said, those people back – they recognize you for who you are back there.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I was afraid to go out and see everybody – anybody, until six months ago or something like that, because . . .

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: You’d sit in this room.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: . . . I didn’t want them to gloat over me or something.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Feel sorry for you and then pity you and all those kinds of things.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah, but it’s not like that.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: But see it’s your attitude that keeps it from being that way. You don’t have that kind of attitude so you not going to get . . .

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: No.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: . . . so you won’t get that kind of a treatment from people.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I know that.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Because it’s like Matt says, you’ve taken it – your stroke in stride. I know a lot of people who’ve had it, and they’ve had that attitude, “Oh, woe is me.”

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I must have done that when I first . . .

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: When you first had it. Sure, but farther on down the road . . .

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah, I got to get on up.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: You got to turn [?] loose. But what did you think after you had your stroke? What did you think? Did you think you would be able to play again? What?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: You don’t think. It’s a long time before you can think. You learn how to eat with . . .

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: It’s the learning process all over?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah, but I think Randy pushed me along.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Before you even – before you came out here?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Oh yeah.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: But when you got here, your mother was still alive. Did she push you too?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Oh yeah, but Randy helped me to get started writing, and so I’m doing it. I’m not writing as fast and all of that as I . . .

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: The quality is there though, Melba.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: . . . I used to, but maybe I’ll get that back in New York, but I don’t have to go as fast, anyway.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: If they want you to write fast, say, “You better get somebody else. If you want something good, then you take me.” What about after your stroke and then you begin to move around and so forth? What did you think about not being able to play your horn? Or did you think about it?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: No. The horn was stolen.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Oh, that’s right.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: So I didn’t think about it, because . . .

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Because it wasn’t there.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Susan . . .

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Susan Slaughter?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Right – got me this horn.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: [?inaudible]

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Maybe.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: You had it about a month ago.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: A month ago. Yeah.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Susan Slaughter from the International Women’s Brass Conference in St. Louis.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah, but she works with the . . .

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Symphony. Kansas – St. Louis Symphony. Trumpet. First chair trumpet and female too. She’s been there how many years? 30? But I thought that was such a nice idea for them to get the trombone and send it to you.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: She said, if you don’t do nothing else, but just sit up and look at it.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Like you did in the window. It’s sitting up there like a mannequin in the window.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: But I do play it – blow two or three notes on it now and then. But this arm here, I got to get going. I don’t know anybody here. Maybe I’ll be doing something on it. But it’s a girl with Ray Charles’s band now.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Playing what?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Playing trombone.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Oh really? Oh please. I haven’t seen her. You just don’t see – there was one girl that was from ’Frisco that was playing with – that was playing in the band when they played your music at the conference. I can’t think of her name, but she was with Diva when they came out here, but I don’t think she’s with them now. I think she went back to school. But she was very good. And then there was a girl in Chicago was very good. She took some solos that night too on some of your music, and she was quite good. Out here on the West Coast, I don’t know of any. But if you said – is that girl with Ray Charles – is she from the West Coast?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: No. She’s just playing jazz about two years, because she was playing symphony before that.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: That’s what the girl in Chicago did too. She was – but she does both now, and she’s quite good. But I’ve got to check the girl out with Ray Charles.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: She’s white. A white girl.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Is she?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: He’s got three trombones.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: You didn’t talk about Janice Robinson?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: No. She was with me. She called me the other day.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Did she really?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: She was talking about taking up the horn again.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: She got married and put it down.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Such a beautiful trombonist.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I told her I was coming back there and I would call her when I came back there. I’m going to get somebody to – not teach me, but sit with me.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Right. Walk you through it, so you can get back to where you were.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I don’t know.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Try to get back to where you were. As long as you make the effort, there’s always a possibility of succeeding. In other words, your future will really begin when you get back to New York. You think?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah, I guess so. Another phase of it, anyway.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Because so to speak it’s been at a standstill since the six or seven years you’ve been here. You’ve written some.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: For Randy, but nobody else.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Didn’t you write something for Al Grey?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Things that I did for me or somebody before.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: But you did five things for me that I haven’t been able to see. I’ve got to get that transcribed.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: [?] is doing them.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Oh really?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: She says . . .

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: I know she gave you a smart answer.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: “How much is I getting?”

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: I’m going to pay her. What does she want?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I said, “You’re going to have to ask” . . .

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Clora.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Because I was giving . . .

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Tell her to come to me and ask – and tell me what she wants, because it’s very important that I . . .

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: She doesn’t know about musicians.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: And friendship.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: You’ve got to get your things out all over the place, and maybe one or two people will do it, but you don’t – paying is not the – that’s not it.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: That’s not the issue.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: It’s not the thing. It’s getting them out as fast and varied.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Like you said, she’s – if they’re not musicians, they do not understand. There’s no way they could understand. And you know what? There’s no way the young girls today can understand the way we understand either.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I don’t think they want to. But anyway, I may be wrong.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: No, because, see, they’re in a position where they don’t feel like they have to go – they know they don’t have to. They’re not going to go through what we went through to get – because there’s almost – we almost put it in their laps.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: There are some girls that are very good. The bass player . . .

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Oh yeah. What’s her name? She played with the Harper brothers and [?] when she was much younger.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Now and then a girl comes along.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Right. That’s true. I have two young girls coming along that’s come to me for private things, and the main thing is to tell them what’s what, who was there, [?], and they understand. So you’re leaving us when now Melba?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I’ll be back in New York for Christmas.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Oh my goodness.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I’m hoping that I’ll be back there, but I might not. I might be here for Christmas. I don’t know.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: But you would like to be there for Christmas. You want all that snow and ice, right?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yep. That’s all right with me.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: You’ve got your friends back there to keep you warm. You have some dedicated friends back there, Melba. No jive. I know I’m dedicated, but you’ve got a whole big bunch of them out – back there.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: That’s wonderful.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: You know what to me, Melba, is people worry about having critical acclaim and all that kind of stuff, but to have my peers recognize me means more to me. I don’t know about you, but it’s always meant more to me than the critics, because I know my peers understand more than the critics do.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Definitely.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: I wanted to get your idea about that.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Your peers – the critics . . .

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Because your peers are not going to leave you like critics will. They’ll praise you one day and the next day, if they’re not feeling too good, they’ll dump you or dump on you or whatever.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I don’t care about the – what do you call them? Peers or something. But my friends – all the guys are my friends. And the girls . . .

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: That’s what I mean. I call them my peers, because we’re doing it in the same business. We’re dedicated just like they are, even though we’re female.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: The girls now – Bu?

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Pleasant?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Bu Pleasant – a saxophonist.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Wilene Martin?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: No, but she – all the . . .

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Fostina Dixon.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah. All them. They’re – we got to get – they’re having a bitch of a time. We got to get something together for the girls. I don’t know how, but we got to get two or three girls here and two or three girls there and things and work it out that they’re out front sometimes and all of that stuff. But I don’t know, because here, it’s not happening, but they might be doing it in New York, Chicago, and places like that. But the girl bass player . . .

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Out here? The one we were talking about?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Um-hmm. And a drummer . . .

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Teri?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Yeah.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Teri Lyne Carrington?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: And who else? I know they got to get out and go back East.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: But Teri left back East. She was there, and she left, and she lives out here now. And I don’t think – I can’t think of the bass player’s name. I don’t know if she’s quite ready to leave her mother. She’s old enough to, but there’s a bond there. Saxophone players? Hmm. Trumpet players: Stacey Rowles. Jimmie’s daughter. And what’s-her­ name that has the big band? [Ann Patterson]. The reed person that has the – what do you call them? It was Roz [?Crans] band first, and then this girl took over the band. She had been doing pretty good with it, because they went to Japan a couple of times. She plays all the reeds, and she’s working somewhere this weekend with that group called the Bandleaders group, or something like that. Everybody in it is a bandleader – Maiden

Voyage – that group. I don’t know any trombone players, [inaudible], but she’s not from out here, you said. Piano players? Young ones? I don’t know. You know, it’s a shame. But really, Melba, it wasn’t that many when we were coming along either, out here. Are there any last remarks that you’d like to give to the young – not just the young girls, but mainly the young girls that are coming along, and young male musicians. I think they have their act kind of together. What do you think?

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: If they’re going to study and do it, do it.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Most of them are.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: And if not, don’t do it.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Don’t even go there.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: That’s all I can say. Don’t get all hung up with nobody other than your music

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Let that be your old man or your old woman or whatever.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Until you know that somebody that’s going to be yours and you’re going to be his, and you’re going to be lifetime or something together.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: And that is a hard nut to crack, learning the difference between lust and love. I have to go through that with my kids, my son. It’s hard. Especially being in show business. You know how everybody’s – we’ve been there.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: But I didn’t do a lot of things. Two guys are kind of [?], but other than that, I was not being low or something, and we made it for years, or something like that.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Because the other night at the concert, my alumni, I kept talking about I had a crush on this one and a crush on that one, and another guy in the audience say, “Looks like you had a crush on everybody.” I said, as long as I just had a crush, that was cool. You can look, but don’t touch. But that is what I try to tell my kids that I’m teaching now. You can admire, but you don’t have to fall for, or whatever, and that is really a big part of being a female in this business, because it’s rough out there. Melba, we’re going to wrap it up, girl. It has been two fantastic days that I’m so glad that I was a part of, because I’ve been wanting to see a complete thing done on you. Maybe we didn’t do it completely, but we almost made it. And I want to thank Smithsonian for giving me a chance to be the one to interview you, because you’ve been such a major part of my life, really, and I’ve just – goose-bump time, your whole

thing. Then when I start to think about how much I have admired you from afar – because you really didn’t know how much until of late. Maybe in the last year we became bonded, but I’ve been bonded to you a long time, and I want – and I really appreciate the chance to sit here and tell you this and be a part of this, what I think has been a fantastic interview, from all the others that I’ve seen. Especially, since you’ve had your stroke, this is just fantastic, Melba, really, and I want you to go back East and get ’em, girl. You go, girl.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: I’m sorry that I couldn’t talk more.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: I know, but you’ve done – you’ve done it. You hear. You’ve done it to death. And I want to say thank you to Matt also for you and I.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: What’s your last name? Watson: Watson.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Oh. Matt Watson.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Yes. Tell Smithsonian we want to thank them for sending a young, handsome man out here, and such a talented one as far as trying to get us to get this interview together, and whatever we’ve done, we owe some of our thanks to Matt for helping us get it together. Melba, you can take over from here. But this – my name is Clora Bryant, and I want to say thank you, Melba Liston.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Okay. And we’ll close with a tune dedicated to my mom and her man, her husband, Ben Loves Lu. [The music plays.] I think maybe this song will be my theme song all over – big band, little band, whatever – if I get everybody to play it like that.

items.speaker: Bryant
items.text: Stay well, Melba.

items.speaker: Liston
items.text: Thank you.
